Q14_1_TEXT: I am extremely sad that we switched from Slack to InScribe. While there are a few extra features that I've appreciated about InScribe (such as the ability to reply to specific replies), the simplicity and lack of overhead of Slack is what made it useful and easy to engage with. It was easy to find class channels, it was easy to see new posts, the interface was simple, there were more reaction options which are fun and engaging. Community engagement plummeted when InScribe was launched, and it's not just because it's new. It's clunky, the layout is confusing, it tries to do too many things, it bombarded me with email notifications, the posts reorder themselves based on replies, and the website itself has a much higher overhead. And this doesn't even begin to touch on the years of help and advice stored within Slack. Often I could search for homework help within Slack and find multiple threads from prior years that immediately solved my issue and helped me learn. If the old Slack content becomes inaccessible, it would be devastating to my learning experience on this degree program. The InScribe experience could become better if more people start to use it, but by this point in the term I think it is clear that it's not popular to use because it's a bad user experience compared to the simplicity of Slack. In Slack I had the feeling of being part of a larger, active community, and InScribe makes me wonder if all of MSDS has only 20 students total.

I believe it would be better if the number of viewers for each thread were not displayed. When the viewer count is visible, the person who posted may feel discouraged, thinking, “So many people saw this, yet I received very few responses.” On the other hand, viewers may assume that someone else will reply and hesitate to respond themselves.

Additionally, when students ask for help, those who want to offer even small pieces of advice may worry that their comments could be interpreted as “giving away answers” or “sharing assignment content,” potentially violating the university’s ethics guidelines. This concern may discourage helpful participation.

To address this, it would be reassuring if the university could provide clear examples of what constitutes an ethics violation and what kinds of advice are considered acceptable. Having concrete guidance would help students feel more comfortable using the bulletin board.

Q11:
Suggestions for improvement fall into two general categories: the InScribe platform and user participation.

In my experience, the InScribe platform's user interface feels disorganized, sparse, and inefficient to use for connecting with fellow users.  To put it briefly, employing an organizational layout like Slack's would be a great improvement.  In the Slack MS-DS community, now archived, individual courses and topics each had their own dedicated channel, which simplified the posting process and improved its accuracy.  Given that each course and topic had its own channel, this made it very easy to ingest information by scrolling and skimming through the chronology of posts related to a specific course/topic in the center panel, and to view replies to posts in the right sidebar.  This made it very quick and easy to find specific information.  The left sidebar provided an efficient and easy way to track one's interests by clearly showing at a glance which channels a user was following, which ones had new posts, any direct messages one might've received, and so on.  The high level of information density visible on screen allowed for quick and easy gleaning of a high concentration of information.

InScribe, on the other hand, organizes posts into one General channel plus several multiple-course specialization channels.  Users can also optionally tag their posts in the General channel with one or more topics.  Unfortunately, sometimes users don't tag their posts at all or tag haphazardly.  When posting to a specialization channel, sometimes students don't indicate which specific course their post is about, or they might post course-specifc questions to the General channel instead of in the relevant specialization channel, which then leads to confusion.  Compared to Slack's organization, where one simply had to post to the relevant channel, InScribe's setup leads to greater inaccuracy in posting and thus makes it harder to follow the stream of relevant posts for a specific course or topic, making it harder to find and follow information on the platform overall.  Furthermore, the information density on screen is too sparse and requires a lot of scrolling to reap the same amount of info that would've been visible on screen at once in Slack's user interface.

I believe that student communities like ours serve two general purposes:  to address students' immediate questions and concerns, whatever they might be, by providing answers and resolutions, and to accumulate this information over time into a knowledge base that future students can reference.  Considering that we are rebuilding our knowledge base from scratch on InScribe (even though we already had a substantial, robust knowledge base on Slack), the aforementioned disorganization inherent to InScribe will result in a knowledge base that is difficult to use, difficult to search effectively to find answers to one's questions, and this disorganization will grow as the knowledge base grows.  As described above, Slack's organizational structure is better suited for building and scaling a useful, efficient, and practical knowledge base over time.

Another concern about the InScribe platform is whether it meets the requirements of the University's digital accessibility policies.  Specifically, some users with certain types of vision impairment, light sensitivity, migraines, etc. benefit from dark mode in managing these conditions when viewing websites on their digital devices.  Currently, InScribe does not offer a dark mode setting, the lack of which negatively impacts users who fall within this group.  Will InScribe be offering dark mode in the near future?

Regarding participation, several students have mentioned that community engagement seems to have diminished since the move to InScribe, and I have noticed the same.  Considering that we are a community of prospective data scientists, could you share usage metrics for the community over time, both from Slack and InScribe, to get a quantitative sense of community engagement?

What might help improve participation?  One of the early December 2025 emails from The Data Science Team, announcing the upcoming move to InScribe, stated that "Moderators will check in to help as needed, but this space is powered by students..."  It's understood that we students are the drivers behind community engagement; however, I think it would help participation if students could feel assured that they can rely on moderators to help consistently and in a timely manner, particularly regarding moderator-originated posts to which a student may have posted a question.  Some moderators have been wonderfully consistent and timely in their responses; other moderators don't respond at all, even as they continue to create new posts (for example, six months have now passed since I asked a question on a moderator's post without a response).  If students begin to feel that they won't receive a response to their questions, then why bother to participate?  If, among various possibilities, this unresponsiveness amounts to ghosting, is this something that the MS-DS program wishes to normalize, considering how unprofessional it is to practice ghosting?

Taking the previous suggestion a step further, I think it would also be helpful if course instructors and staff could participate in the community, to help as needed, particularly when questions arise regarding broken course materials and infrastructure.  This kind of public accountability would help community participation, giving students the assurance that their questions will be addressed, in that they could then see that their concerns are being acknowledged and that the issues will be fixed in a timely manner.  (So far this year, I have seen one course instructor help students in the community in this way, but it seems to be an extreme rarity in the program overall.)  Additionally, considering this from a business perspective, this type of accountability would relieve buyer's remorse and boost morale, knowing that the defective/broken educational product a student purchased will be made whole and that they will get their money's worth from it.  It would also be reassuring to witness tuition revenue streams being clearly reinvested in improving course materials and the MS-DS program overall.

How was the decision made to abandon the Slack community and start over from scratch with InScribe?  Was any student input gathered to substantiate the decision to abandon Slack, just as now you are gathering feedback to support InScribe?  The change from Slack to InScribe felt very sudden, abrupt, and opaque—I believe that this might be a contributing factor to the dissatisfaction some students feel regarding the InScribe community and the abandonment of the Slack community.  

The timing of the change to InScribe felt very premature, in that the Slack knowledge base was still highly relevant and useful to students when the change took place and continues to be so today.  Considering that program courses aren't being updated/fixed very often, for years in some cases, the questions and concerns that students were discussing years ago are still relevant today, and those answers are stored in the Slack knowledge base.  Considering this, why was Slack abandoned when it was?  If a knowledge base must be disposed, it would seem to make sense to do so once the knowledge base is completely obsolete, not while it remains highly relevant and useful.  Once a knowledge base becomes truly obsolete, then it might make sense to switch platforms and start building anew.  I think it might help students if you could explain the substantive underlying rationale for the switch to InScribe from Slack (beyond the marketing materials and hopes expressed in the December 2025 announcement emails).
